title: Factory Method Pattern (creating objects without specifying the exact class)

blocks.text: 9.1.2. Factory Method Pattern

A metrics library ships `public Tag(String name)`, and every service calls `new Tag("region")` on each request. A heap histogram of one service shows about a million `Tag` objects carrying three distinct names. The maintainers want one shared object per name. A constructor can't give them that: `new` always allocates, so the fix is a method in its place, and every call site in every service has to change.

Java has two things called a factory method: a **static factory** returns an instance in place of a constructor, and the **GoF Factory Method** is an overridable method that base-class code calls to create an object, so a subclass decides what gets created.
new Always Allocates; a Static Factory Can Hand Back an Object It Already Made
The library's fix keeps one instance per declared name and makes the constructor private:
A million calls with the three names, each built with `new String(...)` so that no two are the same string object, counting distinct objects:

new Tag(...):  1000000 objects
Tag.of(...):   3 objects

Sharing is safe only because a `Tag` can't change: if one caller could rename a shared tag, every other caller would see it. Names that aren't declared get a fresh object and aren't remembered. A tag name can come from a request header, and a cache keyed by caller input grows with every new value until the heap is full.
The JDK made the same move for the wrappers. `Integer.valueOf` caches -128 to 127 (unit 1.1.1), and the constructor is now marked for removal:
The same program, run as is and then with `-XX:AutoBoxCacheMax=1000`:

new Integer(1000) == new Integer(1000):         false
Integer.valueOf(1000) == Integer.valueOf(1000): false

new Integer(1000) == new Integer(1000):         false
Integer.valueOf(1000) == Integer.valueOf(1000): true

The class files are the same; whether `valueOf(1000)` returns a shared object was decided when the JVM started. A constructor's result is fixed by the language; a factory's only by its javadoc, which for `valueOf` promises -128 to 127 and says it "may cache other values". Code that compares a factory's results with `==` relies on whatever the javadoc leaves open.
<!-- practice 1 -->
A Static Factory Picks the Class From Its Input, So the Class Can Change Without Callers Noticing
`EnumSet.noneOf` declares that it returns an `EnumSet`, an abstract class. Here it is called for an enum of 64 permissions and one of 65:

64 constants: java.util.RegularEnumSet
65 constants: java.util.JumboEnumSet

`RegularEnumSet` keeps the set in one `long`, one bit per constant, which caps it at 64. `JumboEnumSet` keeps a `long[]`. Both are package-private, so no caller can name either; the factory chooses by the enum's size, at every call. Once a 65th permission is deployed, every `EnumSet` of that enum is a `JumboEnumSet`, and no caller's source changes. Had `EnumSet` exposed `new RegularEnumSet<>(Perm.class)`, each call site would be compiled against the 64-bit class, and adding a constant would mean editing all of them. `List.of` picks by size the same way (unit 2.1.2).

The price falls on code that looks at the class: a `getClass()` check, a cast to a concrete type or a serializer keyed by class name breaks when the factory picks another one. A factory promises its declared type, and the class behind it can change between inputs and between JDK releases.
A Constructor Can't Say How It Reads Its Arguments; a Factory's Name Can
`BigDecimal` has a constructor and a static factory that both take a `double`:

new BigDecimal(0.1):     0.1000000000000000055511151231257827021181583404541015625
BigDecimal.valueOf(0.1): 0.1
constructor over the 0.1 limit: true
factory over the 0.1 limit:     false
new BigDecimal(2.675) to cents:     2.67
BigDecimal.valueOf(2.675) to cents: 2.68

The constructor reads the exact binary value of the `double`, which is not 0.1 (unit 1.1.1). `valueOf` reads the `double` the way `Double.toString` prints it, which is the shortest decimal that reads back as the same `double`, so a `double` written as 0.1 prints as 0.1. A fee of 0.1 built with `new` is over a limit of 0.1, and a price of 2.675 rounded half-up comes out a cent short. Both readings have uses, and both take one `double`, so only one of them could be a constructor: constructors have no names of their own, so two with the same parameter list can't coexist (unit 2.1.2 shows the compile error). For amounts, use the `String` constructor or `valueOf(long, int)`; `valueOf(double)` is right only when the `double` came straight from a decimal literal.
The GoF Factory Method Is a Creation Hook That Base-Class Code Calls and a Subclass Overrides

A listener task waits in `ServerSocket.accept()`, and on shutdown we cancel its `Future`. Unit 6.1.3 showed that a platform thread in `accept()` isn't woken by `interrupt()`, so `cancel(true)` returns `true` and the worker stays where it is. Closing the socket would end the wait, but `cancel` belongs to the `Future`, and `submit` creates the `Future` by wrapping the task in a `FutureTask` (unit 6.4.1). It does that through a protected method, `newTaskFor`, which a subclass can override:

The listener is a `Closing<String>` whose `close()` closes its server socket. The caller's code is the same for both pools: `Future<String> f = pool.submit(listener)`, then, once the listener is in `accept()`, `f.cancel(true)`, `shutdown()` and a 500 ms `awaitTermination`:

Executors.newFixedThreadPool(1): cancel=true, worker ended within 500 ms: false
  Executors.newFixedThreadPool(1) accept() ended: java.net.SocketException: Socket closed
  new ClosingExecutor(1) accept() ended: java.net.SocketException: Socket closed
new ClosingExecutor(1)        : cancel=true, worker ended within 500 ms: true

The first pool's worker left `accept()` only when the program closed the socket itself after the wait; in the subclass, `cancel` closed it. `submit`, `invokeAll` and `invokeAny` are written once, in `AbstractExecutorService`, and call `newTaskFor`; the subclass changed the product without touching them or any caller. The base class owns the code that uses the object, and a subclass owns the choice of object, where a static factory makes that choice inside one method.

`submit(Runnable)` goes through the other overload, `newTaskFor(Runnable, T)`. In a pool whose override of the `Callable` overload returns its own product for every task, `submit(() -> "x")` got that product and `submit(() -> { })` a plain `FutureTask`. A subclass overrides every overload its callers can reach. A creation hook called from the base class's constructor runs before the subclass's fields are assigned (unit 2.1.1); `newTaskFor` runs at each `submit`, after construction.
<!-- practice 2 -->
Each Product Costs a Subclass, and the Hook Reaches Only Objects Built From It
The service gets its pools from `Executors`, and the next release moves the listeners to virtual threads. Each pool's class, and whether it is a `ClosingExecutor` (the column `hook overridden`):

java.util.concurrent.ThreadPoolExecutor          hook overridden: false
java.util.concurrent.ThreadPoolExecutor          hook overridden: false
java.util.concurrent.ThreadPerTaskExecutor       hook overridden: false
ClosingExecutor                                  hook overridden: true

`Executors.newFixedThreadPool` and `newCachedThreadPool` build a plain `ThreadPoolExecutor`, which calls its own `newTaskFor`, not the override. `newVirtualThreadPerTaskExecutor()` returns `ThreadPerTaskExecutor`, which doesn't extend `AbstractExecutorService` and has no `newTaskFor` at all. The listener code compiles against all of them unchanged. On the two `ThreadPoolExecutor`s, `cancel` again leaves the worker in `accept()`. On virtual threads the worker ends anyway: Java 21 closes the socket on an interrupt there (unit 6.1.3). But `close()` never runs, so any other cleanup in it is skipped.

The count grows too. A second product, say a task that carries the request id into its logs, is a second subclass with its own `newTaskFor`. A pool that needs both is a third that merges the two overrides, since a class extends one superclass.

The same JDK class shows the other choice. `ThreadPoolExecutor` makes its threads through a `ThreadFactory` passed to its constructor, and most `Executors` methods have an overload that takes one: `Executors.newFixedThreadPool(4, Thread.ofPlatform().name("listener-", 0).factory())` names the threads with no subclass. It can't change the `Future`, which is Challenge 3. A factory passed in works with any creator that accepts it, and can be a lambda (unit 4.1.3). It sees only what the creator hands it, where an override can use the subclass's fields. Keep the hook where the subclass exists for other reasons: every collection must supply its own `iterator()`, and `AbstractCollection` builds `contains`, `remove` and `toString` on it. Choosing an implementation from the class or module path is `ServiceLoader` (unit 8.1.5); one shared instance is unit 9.1.1, and step-by-step construction is unit 9.1.3.
<!-- practice 3 -->
Summary

items: **`new` always allocates; a static factory can hand back an object it already made.** Share only immutable objects, never cache by caller input, and use `==` on the results only where the javadoc promises identity.
**A static factory picks the class from its input.** `EnumSet` switches from `RegularEnumSet` to `JumboEnumSet` at 65 constants with no caller changed; code that checks the class breaks.
**A factory's name says how it reads its arguments.** `new BigDecimal(0.1)` and `BigDecimal.valueOf(0.1)` take the same `double` and return different numbers.
**The GoF factory method is a creation hook.** `submit` calls `newTaskFor`, so one override changes the `Future` for every caller; every overload callers reach must be overridden.

**Each product costs a subclass, and the hook reaches only objects of that subclass.** Pools from `Executors` aren't your subclass, and the virtual-thread executor has no `newTaskFor` at all; a factory passed in reaches any creator that accepts it.

Challenges

items: Your `Money.of(amount, currency)` could cache zero for every currency. Measure what that saves in a service you know, and decide whether callers may then compare with `==` against a `Money.ZERO`.
A library you can't change exposes a public constructor for a class you'd like to share. What can your own code do, and what can't it?
Rewrite `ClosingExecutor` so that it works for any `ExecutorService`, the virtual-thread one included. What does the caller have to change, and what does `invokeAll` lose?

blocks.text: Design Note: Why the Hook and the Parameter Both Survive

GoF's Factory Method comes from the application frameworks of the early 1990s, where the framework's base class ran the algorithm and an application subclassed it to plug in its own objects. Before lambdas, passing a creation object meant an anonymous class, so a subclass hook cost about the same; `newTaskFor` dates from Java 6. Since Java 8 a creation function is cheap to pass, and newer JDK code takes one: `Collectors.toCollection(Supplier)`, `ThreadLocal.withInitial`, `Thread.Builder.factory()`. The hook stays where the creator and the product change together, as a collection and its iterator do. Where the products vary on their own, a parameter saves a creator subclass per product.
